## Method

All participants were recruited through Prolific. Responses were excluded if they were incomplete, flagged by Qualtrics as likely fraudulent, contained a duplicated Prolific ID, or failed the requisite attention checks. Two pilot studies are reported in the Supplementary Materials. The two pre-registered studies used stratified sampling to ensure balanced representation across sex, age, ethnicity (based on simplified U.S. census categories), and political affiliation. The demographic characteristics of the included participants in Study 1 and Study 2 are presented in the Supplementary Materials. 

Study 1 (*N*=`r nrow(Study1)`; pre-registered: <https://aspredicted.org/mv2z-t7dw.pdf>; data collected `r Study1_date`) and Study 2 (*N*=`r nrow(Study2)`; pre-registered: <https://aspredicted.org/z378hg.pdf>; data collected `r Study2_date`) served as the formal replication and extended mediation sample. All data and supplementary materials are publicly accessible on the Open Science Framework (OSF) at: <https://osf.io/qfv9d>. Detailed discrepancies between the pre-registrations and the reported analyses are transparently documented in the Supplementary Materials. Target sample sizes were determined by a priori power analyses detailed in the pre-registration documents. Post-hoc power analyses are detailed in the result section. 

All participants completed the study on Qualtrics. After providing informed consent, they answered a series of questionnaires presented primarily in randomized order to reduce order effects. Demographic questions were administered at the end of the survey.

The primary aim of both pre-registered studies was to test the hypothesis that religiosity, both self-reported and as indexed by behavioral frequency, positively predicts the propensity to seek moral advice and guidance from AI chatbots. Study 1 and Study 2 used the same independent variables (*self-reported religiosity* and *Religious Behavior Score*), and the same primary and secondary outcomes (frequency of and interest in seeking moral advice from AI chatbots, respectively) but differed in the set of candidate mediators examined. The primary outcome was *frequency of seeking moral advice from AI chatbots*. We also assessed participants' *interest in seeking moral advice from AI chatbots* as a secondary outcome, whose results largely mirror those for Frequency and are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

To assess participants' broader disposition to moral consultation, both studies measured frequency of and interest in seeking moral advice from 18 sources. To compute each composite, we averaged across 13 non-AI, non-religious sources. Five sources were excluded to avoid criterion contamination with the outcome (“Chatbots/ AI assistants”) and predictor (three explicitly religious sources), and because internal deliberation (“Yourself”) does not constitute external guidance.

Following the theoretical framework outlined in the Introduction, candidate mediators were organized into six clusters: (a) moral consultation disposition (overall frequency of and interest in seeking moral advice from non-AI, non-religious sources); (b) epistemic humility (moral curiosity using the Moral Curiosity Scale [@hartman2022], general curiosity using the Curiosity and Exploration Inventory-II [@kashdan2009], and intellectual humility assessed via the Multidimensional Intellectual Humility Scale [@alfano2017] and the Comprehensive Intellectual Humility Scale [@krumrei-mancuso2016]); (c) moral objectivism (*belief in moral objectivity*); (d) positive perception of AI chatbots (*perceived authority of AI chatbots as moral advisors*, and in Study 1 only, *perceived valence of AI chatbots as moral advisors*); (e) *tendency to anthropomorphize AI chatbots* (assessed via the adapted Anthropomorphism Subscale of the Godspeed Questionnaire [@bartneck2009]; Study 2 only); and (f) other personality traits (Study 2 only; *fear of negative judgment* using the Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale [@leary1983], *self-reflective tendency* using the Self-Reflection and Insight Scale [@grant2002], and *deference to authority* using the Moral Foundations Questionnaire [MFQ-2; @atari2023] and the Morality-as-Cooperation Questionnaire [MAC-Q; @curry2019]). Study 1 tested clusters (a)–(d). Study 2 retained clusters (a)–(d) and added clusters (e)–(f). The Supplementary Materials summarize all variables used across the two pre-registered studies.
